analysis.one_liner: Makes online marketplaces legally responsible for counterfeit health-and-safety goods sold by their third-party sellers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support, the bill got a referral to the Senate Judiciary Committee and one subcommittee hearing in October 2023, then died without a floor vote when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Trademark Act so that online shopping platforms can be sued when a third-party seller on their site uses a counterfeit brand on a product that can hurt someone's health — things like medicine, car parts, toys, or electronics. Platforms can avoid that liability if they take specific steps: verify sellers, screen listings before they go live, remove flagged fakes quickly, and ban repeat counterfeiters. The rules apply to platforms with at least $500,000 in annual sales, with smaller platforms swept in after ten valid counterfeit notices. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday online shoppers, especially anyone buying products where a fake could cause real harm — medicines, children's products, electronics, auto parts, cosmetics. Trademark owners also gain a practical enforcement tool: instead of chasing thousands of anonymous counterfeit sellers, they can demand platforms screen and remove listings, and sue platforms that fail to act. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Platforms become contributorily liable when a third-party seller uses a counterfeit mark on a good that implicates health and safety, giving shoppers a party with real resources to hold accountable. [S2]

Platforms escape liability only if they take defined preventive steps: verify each seller's US registered agent, require accurate product images, screen listings before display at no charge to brand owners, remove flagged listings quickly, terminate repeat counterfeiters (three strikes in a year is the benchmark), and stop banned sellers from rejoining under aliases. [S2]

Small platforms under $500,000 in annual sales are exempt unless they rack up ten qualifying counterfeit notices, and courts must weigh a platform's size and resources when judging whether its measures were reasonable. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: E-commerce platforms — from giants to mid-sized marketplaces — bear the compliance costs of seller verification, screening, and takedown programs, plus new litigation exposure when counterfeit health-and-safety goods slip through. Some of those costs could be passed on to sellers in fees, and platforms argue the burden is heavy. Trademark owners also must supply the notice information and points of contact the screening system depends on. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The screening and takedown system depends on brand owners providing notice information; the bill relieves platforms from liability when registrants do not provide it, so enforcement could be uneven depending on which brands participate. [S2]

Automated screening before listings go public risks sweeping up legitimate listings; the bill gives sellers a chance to prove their goods are genuine, but appeals and reinstatement take time and platforms will likely err on the side of removal. [S2]

New liability exposure and compliance programs carry real costs for platforms, and a good-faith objection is that large marketplaces already operate anti-counterfeit programs, so a federal liability standard adds litigation risk without proportional added protection. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a shopper buying medicine or a child's car seat online, the benefit is concrete: a legal mechanism that pushes platforms to actively screen out dangerous fakes rather than disclaim responsibility. The costs fall mainly on the platforms, which are well positioned to absorb them, though smaller marketplaces and legitimate sellers caught up in automated screening face genuine friction. On balance the bill's protection is targeted at goods where counterfeits can injure people, and it builds in a safe harbor so compliant platforms are not sued — a reasonable design, but one that never got a test.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing in October 2023, and sat there until the Congress ended with no committee vote and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Coons introduced the bill on September 26, 2023, joined by Sen. Tillis, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day. [S4] [S2]
The bill had two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat. [S3]
On October 3, 2023, the Judiciary Committee's Intellectual Property Subcommittee held a hearing on the bill — its only recorded action beyond referral. [S4]
No further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025; the full committee never voted and the Senate never considered the bill. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online marketplaces are better off because the bill died: they carry no new federal liability for counterfeit health-and-safety goods sold on their sites and face no mandated screening, takedown, or repeat-seller-ban programs. Shoppers continue to bear the risk of buying counterfeits online, and brand owners keep relying on the patchwork of private enforcement that exists today.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Coons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its prior versions' approach; brought it to the Judiciary Committee's Intellectual Property Subcommittee, which held a hearing on it in October 2023. [S2] [S4]

for.name: Sen. Thom Tillis
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, making the sponsorship bipartisan from day one. [S2] [S3]

against.name: E-commerce platforms
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanding platform liability for third-party counterfeits when versions of this proposal circulated publicly, arguing their existing anti-counterfeit programs make a new liability standard unnecessary and that it would raise costs and invite litigation.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from introduction — a Democratic sponsor joined by a Republican original cosponsor, with the two cosponsors split one from each party [S3] — and no recorded opposition ever developed on the floor because the bill never got that far.

industries.note: The bill creates a new route to sue platforms over third-party counterfeit goods and requires them to run seller verification, pre-publication screening, takedown, and repeat-infringer ban programs at no charge to brand owners. Platforms argue they already police fakes voluntarily; the bill would convert that discretion into a legal duty backed by liability. [S2]

The bill gives them a lever over the platforms where their products are counterfeited: notice-based screening, required takedowns, and a way to sue platforms that fail to act. Their gain comes alongside consumer safety rather than at consumers' expense. [S2]

Sellers of fake goods face mandatory screening before listings go live, rapid removal once flagged, termination after repeated violations, and being blocked from returning under new identities. Their business model depends on the anonymity the bill is designed to remove. [S2]
